narrative:
The model estimated a 55.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first try. That is only slightly more likely than passing, but it was high enough to cross the school’s risk threshold, so your application was denied. This is a prediction, not a certainty. Your gender and race were not used in this decision.

The denial was driven mainly by your third-year class-rank decile. You were in decile 1, while accepted students averaged around decile 5.8, and this was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor. At 36, it was slightly below the accepted-student average of 37.18, yet in your full profile it pushed toward passing and was the main point in your favor. Family income was the third most important factor: coming from a middle-income bracket modestly pushed the prediction toward failure.

To improve your position, ask the admissions office for feedback and whether reapplying is possible. If feasible, retake the LSAT and aim for a clearly stronger score. Also seek advice on strengthening your academic record or explaining your low third-year rank, and consider delaying reapplication until you can show evidence that reduces the predicted bar-exam risk.
